newsitem.title: UK: Euro crude outlook - Contango to stay but narrower.
newsitem.headline: Euro crude outlook - Contango to stay but narrower.

text.p: The steep contango at the front end of the benchmark Brent crude market looks set to roll forward for a while this week, but improving refining margins and perceptions of a squeeze play on early April barrels may offer support, traders said.
Overall traders see continuing weak North Sea numbers early in the week until the market absorbs late March grades including a couple of late March Brents.
But longer term bulls feel more confident.

"Once you get into late April values will get better," a trader said. "The wet players at the front end of the market are mesmerised by the current overhang. Big deal. In a week or so it will all be gone and the numbers will improve."
"I'm not bearish but I'm also not extremely bullish either," said another trader.
"We're seeing better margins and that should encourage refiners to take in more crude," he added.
Some sellers said they detected improved interest for April barrels, particularly those with high gasoline yields.
March 29-31 Brent fetched April Brent -90 cents a barrel last week, worth a bearish May Brent -77 cents, but traders said most attention was switching to early April wet values.

U.K. major BP was holding all 10 Brents due to load in the first six days of April on Friday, having collected two April 4-6 stems clocked to Phibro and Aron in "late passes" last Thursday and kept all three cargoes turning wet on Friday.
However, a senior trader at a European major expressed concern that the Brent market could continue soft if BP's April cargoes have not found homes early in the week.

Forward price indicators CFDs for this week were trading around May futures -48 to -50 cents on Friday, flagging trader sentiment that the potential a squeeze on early April barrels could cause a short-term price spike on the 15-day Brent market.
Traders said BP may be looking to push prices up in order to optimise profits on delivery tolerances.

They said this could prompt bearish shorts to roll positions forward, thus putting a bottom to the market for a while. But some traders felt there may eventually be a need to cover those positions, particularly if the U.S. arbitrage opens up and there is further evidence that European refiners are increasing crude runs again.
Traders also said that fund interest could be switching more to commodities as worries over interest rates rises hit stock markets on both sides of the Atlantic.

On the trans-Atlantic front U.S. Gulf Coast refiners continue to enjoy an array of choices when looking to fill their needs, with West African and North Sea crudes on offer in competition with domestic grades.
U.S. traders said they expected the surplus crudes to be absorbed in the coming weeks, possibly leading to short-term tightness.
"If the floods in Louisiana cause problems for pipelines, then you could see, in maybe a week or 10 days, people wondering why May/June Brent is at plus 40 cts," a trader said.
However, with Brent having to compete with ample West African avails into U.S. Gulf, traders said arbitrage options would remain limited.
"You would have to swallow 15-20 cents to make Brent work into the U.S. Gulf at the moment," one trader said.

European refineries are feeling more confident about profit margins and at least two have decided to restore crude runs after cuts early this month, but traders continued to seek fresh trans-Atlantic arbitrage for real fundamental support.
Margins for a complex Rotterdam refinery have risen to $1.14 a barrel compared with 80 cents at the beginning of the month, according to Reuters price data using standard product yields.
-- Colin Wooster, London Newsroom, +44 171 5420 7456
